topic: The Pi Collision Puzzle: Calculating Pi through Physics
target_audience: High school students and university undergraduates with basic physics and geometry knowledge

sections.title: Introduction: The Impossible Connection
sections.content: Introduce a simple physical scenario: a wall, a small block (mass m), and a large block (mass M). The large block slides toward the small block, which is sitting between the wall and the large block. Ask the audience: 'How many times will these objects collide?'
sections.example: Imagine a tiny mouse (mass m) sitting between a wall and a giant elephant (mass M) riding a skateboard. Every time the elephant hits the mouse, or the mouse hits the wall, we count it as one 'clack'.

sections.title: Setting the Rules: Elastic Collisions
sections.content: Define the physical constraints. 1. No friction. 2. Perfectly elastic collisions (kinetic energy and momentum are conserved). 3. The wall is immovable. Introduce the variables for velocity and mass.
sections.example: Visualize the blocks as frictionless pucks on an air-hockey table. Use color-coded vectors (arrows) to show the velocity of each block after every 'clack'.

sections.title: The Pattern Emerges: Counting the Clacks
sections.content: Demonstrate the results for different mass ratios. When M = m, there are 3 collisions. When M = 100m, there are 31 collisions. When M = 10,000m, there are 314 collisions. Highlight the appearing digits of Pi.
sections.example: Show a digital counter above the blocks. Ratio 1:1 -> '3'. Ratio 100:1 -> '31'. Ratio 1,000,000:1 -> '3141'. The audience should see the digits of Pi appearing as M increases by powers of 100.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws as Geometry
sections.content: Explain that conservation of energy (1/2 Mv² + 1/2 mu² = E) represents an ellipse in a velocity-space graph (v, u). By rescaling the x-axis by sqrt(M), the ellipse transforms into a perfect circle.
sections.example: An animation morphing a stretched-out oval (ellipse) into a perfect circle by scaling the 'Big Block Velocity' axis. This circle represents all possible states of the system.

sections.title: The Geometric Insight: The Bouncing Beam
sections.content: Map each collision to a point on the circle. A block-block collision follows momentum conservation, which looks like a reflection across a specific line. A wall collision (changing direction of the small block) is a reflection across the u-axis.
sections.example: Show a laser beam bouncing inside a circular mirror. Each time the beam hits the edge of the circle, it represents one collision in the real world. The total number of collisions is the number of 'hits' before the beam exits the arc.

sections.title: The Grand Conclusion: Why Pi?
sections.content: Explain that as the mass ratio M/m becomes very large, the angle of each 'bounce' on the circle becomes very small. The total number of collisions is the total arc length covered divided by the step size, which leads directly to the formula involving Pi.
sections.example: Overlay a circle of radius 1 onto the block simulation. Show that the total number of steps is equal to the circumference (2π) divided by the tiny angle θ, which is approximately the square root of the mass ratio.

sections.title: Summary and Takeaway
sections.content: Recap how a purely kinetic counting puzzle reveals a fundamental mathematical constant. Emphasize that Pi isn't just about circles, but about the deep symmetry in conservation laws.
sections.example: A final side-by-side shot: the blocks finishing their collisions on one side, and the digits of Pi (3.1415...) glowing on the other, linked by a circular arc.
